chapters.title: Chapter 1: What You Actually Own in a Startup

lessons.title: What Startup Equity Really Is: Shares, Ownership and Your Claim on the Company

children.text: A college friend is raising money for her coffee brand and texts you: "Put in ₹5 lakh and I'll give you 1% of the company." It sounds simple. It is not. 1% of what? How many shares exist today? How many will exist after the next round? What kind of share is it, and what can you actually do with it? This lesson gives you the vocabulary to answer those questions before your money leaves your bank account.

body.text: When you invest in a startup, you do not buy a rupee value. You buy a number of shares. Your ownership is your shares divided by all the shares that exist, and that bottom number keeps growing.

children.text: A Startup Is a Company, and a Company Is Divided Into Shares
Almost every Indian startup that raises outside money is a
private limited company
under the Companies Act, 2013. At incorporation, the founders decide how many shares to create and their
face value
, and each founder takes some of them.

markDefs.definition: A company registered under the Companies Act, 2013 that restricts share transfers through its Articles, limits members to 200 (excluding current and certain former employees) and cannot invite the public to buy its shares.
The nominal value of each share, usually ₹1 or ₹10. It has almost nothing to do with what the share is actually worth.

children.text: A share is a unit of ownership. Hold shares and you become a shareholder, legally called a member, with a claim on the company in proportion to how many shares you hold. That proportion is the only number that really matters.

body.caption: Your stake is always a fraction, never a fixed rupee amount

children.text: Worked Example: Meera Invests in ChaiCart

ChaiCart Technologies Private Limited is a fictional Pune startup running app-based tea kiosks. Co-founders Ananya and Vikram incorporated it with 10,000 equity shares of face value ₹10 each. Ananya took 6,000 and Vikram took 4,000.

A year later, Meera, a product manager in Bengaluru, agrees to invest ₹20 lakh at ₹800 per share. ChaiCart does not hand her any of the founders' shares. It issues 2,500 brand new shares to her, and the total rises from 10,000 to 12,500.

body.caption: ChaiCart shareholding before and after Meera invests

body.text: Look at what did not change: Ananya still holds exactly 6,000 shares. Her stake fell from 60% to 48% only because the total number of shares grew. That is dilution, and you will see it in every funding round for the rest of this course.

children.text: Meera paid ₹800 for a share with a face value of ₹10. The extra ₹790 per share is
securities premium
. In startup rounds, the premium is almost the entire price.

markDefs.definition: The amount an investor pays above face value. It is recorded in a separate reserve on the balance sheet, not in share capital.

children.text: ChaiCart's balance sheet records Meera's ₹20 lakh in two places:
Share capital:
Securities premium:
Total received:

This is why a startup can show paid-up capital of just ₹1.25 lakh (12,500 shares × ₹10) on the MCA portal while having raised far more. Paid-up share capital counts only face value. Always look at the securities premium as well.

body.title: What is the whole company worth?
body.prompt: Meera paid ₹800 per share, and ChaiCart now has 12,500 shares in total. At that price, what is the whole company worth, in ₹ lakh?
body.explanation: 12,500 × ₹800 = ₹1,00,00,000, which is ₹100 lakh or ₹1 crore. Meera's ₹20 lakh buys 20% of a ₹1 crore company. Chapter 2 formalises this as post-money valuation.

children.text: Your Percentage Falls, and That Can Be Good News

Eighteen months later, ChaiCart raises ₹1 crore in its Series A at ₹3,200 per share, issuing 3,125 new shares. Total shares rise to 15,625. Meera did not sell a single share, but her position has changed.

A smaller slice of a much bigger cake. Dilution at a higher share price is healthy. Dilution at a lower price, called a down round, is where investors get hurt, and Chapter 4 covers it. Also notice the words "on paper". That ₹80 lakh is simply the last round's price multiplied by Meera's shares. She cannot sell it on NSE tomorrow morning.

body.label: Sachin Bansal's Flipkart stake at exit
body.context: When Walmart bought about 77% of Flipkart for roughly $16 billion in 2018, co-founder Sachin Bansal reportedly sold his entire stake of about 5.5% for around $1 billion. Eleven years of dilution took his percentage down to single digits, and it was still a life-changing outcome.

children.text: What Your Shares Actually Give You
An equity share in an Indian private company carries four core entitlements. Each one comes with a catch when you are a small investor.

body.caption: The rights attached to an equity share
headers: The catch for a small angel

cells: Votes on resolutions at general meetings, in proportion to your paid-up equity capital
At 1% to 5%, your vote rarely changes an outcome
A share of profits when a dividend is declared
Loss-making startups almost never pay one
Whatever is left after everyone else is paid if the company winds up
In a failed startup, usually nothing is left
Annual financial statements, notices of general meetings and access to statutory registers
Monthly MIS and investor updates come only if your shareholders' agreement promises them

children.text: Voting power works in thresholds, and these three numbers come up constantly in Indian deal negotiations.

stats.label: Passes special resolutions
stats.context: Altering the Articles, issuing shares to new investors

stats.label: Can block special resolutions
stats.context: Why founders watch this number closely

children.text: Where Equity Sits When Things Go Wrong

Equity is the riskiest claim on a company because it is paid last. If a startup is liquidated under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, the money raised from selling its assets flows down a fixed order of priority. Simplified from Section 53:
Liquidation costs.
The fees and expenses of running the liquidation itself.
Secured lenders and workmen's dues.
Banks or venture debt funds holding security, alongside unpaid dues to workmen.
Employees, then unsecured lenders.
Other unpaid salaries, followed by lenders without security.
Government dues and remaining creditors.
Taxes, any unpaid secured amounts and other debts such as vendor bills.
Preference shareholders.
Investors holding preference shares.
Equity shareholders.
Whatever is left, if anything, shared in proportion to shareholding.

body.text: A big headline valuation does not protect equity holders. Byju's was valued at about $22 billion in 2022, and by 2024 its parent company was in insolvency proceedings, with creditors ahead of every shareholder in the queue. A valuation is what the last investor paid, not what you will get back.

body.title: Who gets paid?
body.question: ChaiCart shuts down. After selling its kiosks and paying liquidation costs, ₹40 lakh is left. It owes a bank ₹25 lakh (secured), staff ₹8 lakh in unpaid salaries and vendors ₹10 lakh. How much reaches Meera and the founders?
options: ₹8 lakh, which is 20% of ₹40 lakh, to Meera
Whatever remains after the bank alone is repaid
body.explanation: Creditors are owed ₹43 lakh (₹25 lakh + ₹8 lakh + ₹10 lakh), more than the ₹40 lakh available. The bank takes ₹25 lakh, staff take ₹8 lakh and vendors get the last ₹7 lakh. Shareholders receive nothing, because equity is paid only after every creditor is paid in full.

children.text: A Startup Share Is Not a Listed Share

columns.label: Eternal (formerly Zomato) shares bought on NSE via Zerodha
points: Price discovered continuously during market hours
Sell on any trading day, with T+1 settlement
Quarterly results and ongoing disclosures under SEBI LODR rules
Anyone with a demat account can buy a single share

columns.label: ChaiCart shares bought in a funding round
points: Price set once per funding round
No exchange to sell on, and transfers are restricted
Disclosures depend largely on what your agreement promises
Cheques typically start in the lakhs
Investors often receive CCPS instead of equity shares (Lesson 1.3)

children.text: The selling restrictions come from two documents: the company's
Articles of Association
and the
shareholders' agreement
. Read both before you sign anything.

markDefs.definition: The company's internal rulebook, filed with the Registrar of Companies. A private company's Articles must restrict the transfer of its shares.
A private contract between the company and its shareholders setting investor rights such as information rights, board seats, transfer restrictions and exit terms.

children.text: Most private companies, other than small companies, are now required to issue and hold their shares in demat form, so your startup shares may sit in the same demat account you use with Zerodha or Groww. Being in demat does not make them tradeable. There is still no exchange to sell them on.

body.label: MCA: View Company or LLP Master Data
body.description: Search a startup by name or CIN to check its registration status, incorporation date, authorised capital and paid-up capital before you invest.

body.title: The "1% for ₹5 lakh" message
body.scenario: Your college friend Riya runs BrewBox, a Mumbai-based direct-to-consumer coffee brand. She messages you: "We're raising our angel round. Put in ₹5 lakh and you get 1% of the company. Paperwork is simple, I'll sort it out later."
body.prompt: Write down every question you would ask before transferring any money.
body.modelAnswer:
1. How many shares exist today, and how many will I be issued? "1%" means nothing without a share count.
2. Is that 1% before or after this round, and does it account for the ESOP pool and any convertible notes? (Lessons 1.2 and 3.3)
3. What is the price per share, and what company value does it imply? ₹5 lakh for 1% implies ₹5 crore.
4. What class of share am I getting: equity shares or CCPS? (Lesson 1.3)
5. Where are the documents? A share subscription agreement, shareholders' agreement and updated Articles should exist before money moves, not "later".
6. Will the shares be allotted in demat form, and will the company file the return of allotment (Form PAS-3) with the MCA? Ask for a copy once the round closes.

body.title: The queue
body.textWithBlank: If a company is liquidated, equity shareholders are paid ___, after every creditor and preference shareholder.
body.explanation: Equity holds the residual claim. It gets only what remains after creditors and preference shareholders are paid in full, which in a failed startup is usually nothing.

cards.definition: A unit of ownership in a company. Your stake is your shares divided by total shares outstanding.
The nominal value of a share, usually ₹1 or ₹10, unrelated to what the share is worth.
The amount paid above face value, recorded separately from share capital.
The fall in your ownership percentage when a company issues new shares to others.
Equity's right to whatever is left after all creditors and preference shareholders are paid.
A shareholder decision needing at least 75% of votes cast, such as altering the Articles.
Your shares multiplied by the last round price. It is not cash until someone buys your shares.

points: You buy shares, not a percentage. Ownership equals your shares divided by total shares outstanding.
Funding rounds issue new shares, so existing holders' percentages fall even though their share counts do not change.
Dilution at a higher share price can raise the value of your stake. Dilution at a lower price hurts.
Face value is nominal. Startup investors pay mostly securities premium.
Equity shareholders vote, may receive dividends and hold the residual claim, but they are paid last in a liquidation.
Startup shares cannot be sold like NSE-listed shares. Transfers are restricted and valuations stay on paper until an exit.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. ChaiCart and BrewBox are fictional companies used for illustration. Startup investments are high risk, illiquid and can result in the loss of your entire capital. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before investing.
